claim: Mutations in the lever arm of β-cardiac myosin are a frequent cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by hypercontractility and eventual hypertrophy of the left ventricle.
source: Mutations in the lever arm of β-cardiac myosin are a frequent cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a disease characterized by hypercontractility and eventual hypertrophy of the left ventricle.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the disease characteristics, supported by citation (Ho et al., 2009) in the introduction.

claim: Mutations in the lever arm of β-cardiac myosin have divergent allosteric effects on myosin function, depending on whether they are in the pliant or light chain-binding regions.
source: Thus, mutations in the lever arm of β-cardiac myosin have divergent allosteric effects on myosin function, depending on whether they are in the pliant or light chain-binding regions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The myosin lever arm was first recognized almost 30 years ago.
source: The myosin lever arm was first recognized almost 30 years ago as the first structure of myosin subfragment 1 (S1) was described (Rayment et al., 1993a; Rayment et al., 1993b)
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citations to Rayment et al., 1993a and 1993b.

claim: The lever arm's function in amplifying the motion of the converter domain was confirmed.
source: and the lever arm's function in amplifying the motion of the converter domain was subsequently confirmed (Uyeda et al., 1996; Geeves and Holmes, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uyeda et al., 1996 and Geeves and Holmes, 1999.

claim: HCM-causing mutations in the myosin motor domain have been described and characterized.
source: While many HCM-causing mutations in the myosin motor domain have been described and characterized (Nag et al., 2015; Adhikari et al., 2016; Kawana et al., 2017; Nag et al., 2017; Adhikari et al., 2019; Sarkar et al., 2020; Vander Roest et al., 2021; Spudich, 2019; Liu et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: HCM-causing mutations in the lever arm remain understudied.
source: HCM-causing mutations in the lever arm remain understudied, despite the fact that the lever arm has a relatively high rate of these mutations and plays a key role in transducing the chemical energy of ATP hydrolysis into physical motion (Uyeda et al., 1996; Geeves and Holmes, 1999)
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citations.

claim: HCM affects up to 1 in 200 in the US population.
source: HCM is a leading cause of genetic heart disease, affecting up to 1 in 200 in the US population (Semsarian et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a statistical claim supported by citation to Semsarian et al., 2015.

claim: The vast majority of HCM mutations occur in either the β-cardiac myosin heavy chain or cardiac myosin-binding protein-C.
source: Mutations leading to HCM have been found in genes encoding a variety of sarcomeric proteins; however, the vast majority occur in either the β-cardiac myosin heavy chain or cardiac myosin-binding protein-C (Konno et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Konno et al., 2010.

claim: Left ventricular hypercontractility typically precedes hypertrophy in HCM patients.
source: Because left ventricular hypercontractility typically precedes hypertrophy in HCM patients (Ho et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation to Ho et al., 2009.

claim: It has been hypothesized that sarcomeric mutations lead to hypercontractility at the molecular scale.
source: it has been hypothesized that sarcomeric mutations lead to hypercontractility at the molecular scale
evidence: This is a hypothesis statement based on the field's understanding.

claim: Many HCM-causing mutations appear to reduce myosin's ability to form an autoinhibited state.
source: lately, a more compelling hypothesis has gained traction: many HCM-causing mutations appear to reduce myosin's ability to form an autoinhibited state (Nag et al., 2017; Adhikari et al., 2019; Sarkar et al., 2020; Vander Roest et al., 2021; Spudich, 2019; Moore et al., 2012; Spudich, 2015; Alamo et al., 2017; Robert-Paganin et al., 2018; Anderson et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of an autoinhibited state could lead to additional myosin heads acting to generate force during contraction, thus leading to hypercontractility.
source: Loss of an autoinhibited state could lead to additional myosin heads acting to generate force during contraction, thus leading to hypercontractility.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the understanding of myosin autoinhibition.

claim: An autoinhibited state of myosin was first described in smooth muscle myosin over 20 years ago.
source: An autoinhibited state of myosin was first described in smooth muscle myosin over 20 years ago (Trybus, 1991)
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citation to Trybus, 1991.

claim: The relevance of the autoinhibited state to β-cardiac myosin and HCM was only more recently recognized.
source: but its relevance to β-cardiac myosin and HCM was only more recently recognized
evidence: This is a statement about the timeline of scientific understanding.

claim: In the interacting heads motif, one of the two heads has its actin-binding interface buried in the folded structure and is referred to as the 'blocked head'.
source: One of the two heads in the dimer has its actin-binding interface buried in the folded structure; this head is referred to as the 'blocked head', while the other is called the 'free head', since its actin-binding interface is not hidden structurally.
evidence: This is a description of the IHM structure based on structural studies cited (Wendt et al., 2001; Woodhead et al., 2005).

claim: Many myosin types have been shown to assume the folded back IHM structure.
source: Many myosin types have been shown to assume this folded back IHM structure (Woodhead et al., 2005; Jung et al., 2008; Al-Khayat et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: The IHM structure is thought to be a common feature across the myosin II class.
source: and it is now thought to be a common feature across the myosin II class (Lee et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: The IHM structure has been correlated to an ultra-low basal ATPase rate in the absence of actin called the 'super relaxed state' (SRX).
source: The IHM structure has been correlated to an ultra-low basal ATPase rate (three orders of magnitude below the actin-activated ATPase rate) in the absence of actin called the 'super relaxed state' (SRX; Anderson et al., 2018; Al-Khayat et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2010; McNamara et al., 2015; Rohde et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Heads lacking the S2 tail mostly have a faster basal ATPase rate referred to as the 'disordered relaxed state' (DRX).
source: Heads lacking the S2 tail mostly have a faster basal ATPase rate (two orders of magnitude below the actin-activated ATPase rate) referred to as the 'disordered relaxed state' (DRX).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional state of myosin without the S2 tail, based on established knowledge.

claim: When the S2 tail is present, the apparent ATPase rate decreases, suggesting that the S2 tail promotes autoinhibition.
source: Additionally, actin-activated ATPases comparing myosin with and without its S2 tail have shown that when the S2 tail is present, the apparent ATPase rate decreases, suggesting that the S2 tail promotes autoinhibition (Nag et al., 2017; Adhikari et al., 2019; Sarkar et al., 2020; Vander Roest et al., 2021; Trybus et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: There may be circumstances in which the structural states are uncoupled from their respective rates.
source: While these structural states are correlated to specific basal and actin-activated ATPase rates, there may be circumstances in which the structural states are uncoupled from their respective rates (Chu et al., 2021; Nag and Trivedi, 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chu et al., 2021 and Nag and Trivedi, 2021.

claim: Three joints in the molluscan myosin lever arm appear to be potential sources of flexibility which may be necessary for the formation of the IHM.
source: A number of structural studies collectively concluded that three joints in the molluscan myosin lever arm appear to be potential sources of flexibility which may be necessary for the formation of the IHM (Houdusse et al., 2000; Houdusse and Cohen, 1996; Himmel et al., 2009; Pylypenko and Houdusse, 2011; Brown et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies on molluscan myosin.

claim: High-resolution cryo-EM structures of the folded-back IHM state in smooth muscle myosin demonstrated that the lever arm must take on a different conformation in each of the asymmetric folded heads in the IHM.
source: Recently, high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the folded-back IHM state in smooth muscle myosin demonstrated that the lever arm must take on a different conformation in each of the asymmetric folded heads in the IHM, further confirming the importance of lever arm positioning in the folded state (Scarff et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Heissler et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent cryo-EM studies.

claim: Several previous studies investigating RLC mutations have suggested that mutations can modulate lever arm compliance.
source: Indeed, several previous studies investigating RLC mutations have suggested that mutations can modulate lever arm compliance (Greenberg et al., 2010; Sherwood et al., 2004; Karabina et al., 2015; Farman et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on RLC mutations.

claim: The 'hook' or 'ankle' joint near the C-terminus of the lever arm is common across the myosin II class and can bend to very different angles.
source: Another region that has been identified as important in molluscan myosin is the 'hook' or 'ankle' joint near the C-terminus of the lever arm (Pylypenko and Houdusse, 2011; Brown et al., 2011). This feature is common across the myosin II class and can bend to very different angles, which is thought to help allow for the folded back conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The F834L mutation is very close to the ankle joint.
source: The F834L mutation is very close to that ankle joint, and thus could affect the conformation about that joint (Fig. S7H)
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claim: A high-resolution structure of human β-cardiac myosin in the IHM state will be useful to further understand the structural requirements of the lever arm for autoinhibition.
source: In any case, a high-resolution structure of human β-cardiac myosin in the IHM state will be useful to further understand the structural requirements of the lever arm for autoinhibition.

claim: The pliant region seems to play an intriguing role in both transducing force from the motor domain to the lever arm and potentially forming the IHM structure.
source: With a high density of mutations across a very small region of myosin, the pliant region seems to play an intriguing role in both transducing force from the motor domain to the lever arm and potentially forming the IHM structure.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results.
